facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Having conquered him, Ravana exterminated four hundred of the Daityas in less than an hour, slaying Vidyutjihva in the tumult of battle.
facts.text: In the Uttara Kanda of the Valmiki Ramayana, Ravana kills his own brother-in-law, Vidyutjihva, the prince of the Danavas and husband of Surpanakha, during his conquest of the subterranean city of Ashmanagar.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Ravana consoled his weeping sister and sent her to reside in the Dandaka forest alongside Khara and fourteen thousand fierce warriors.
facts.text: Ravana appeased the inconsolable, newly widowed Surpanakha by assigning her to live in the Dandaka forest under the military guard of their half-brother Khara and fourteen thousand rakshasas.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Rama then voicing clearly and softly spoke to her, whom the noose of lust has tethered down, with a smile preceding his words.
facts.text: In the Aranya Kanda of the Valmiki Ramayana, Surpanakha arrives at Panchavati, becomes enamored by Rama, and explicitly asks him to abandon Sita and take her as his wife.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: This is my younger brother, named Lakshmana, of good conduct and pleasing to look upon... he is without a wife and would make a husband well suited to your beauty.
facts.text: Valmiki records that Rama and Lakshmana playfully redirected Surpanakha between one another with verbal jesting before any violence occurred.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Today I shall devour this human woman before your eyes; without a co-wife, I will roam happily with you.
facts.text: According to Valmiki's Sanskrit text, Lakshmana disfigured Surpanakha only after she flew into a rage and lunged forward to kill and eat Sita.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: The valiant Lakshmana, highly incensed against the Rakshasi, thereupon drew his sword from its scabbard and, in the presence of Rama, cut off her ears and nose.
facts.text: Under Rama's explicit instruction to suppress the violent attacker, Lakshmana drew his sword and severed both Surpanakha's nose and ears.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Lakshmana, holding a sword in his upraised right hand and the hair of Surpanakha in his left is about to mutilate her in the presence of Rama and Sita.
facts.source_name: ASI, Memoirs of the Archaeological Survey of India No. 70
facts.text: An excavated 5th-century CE Gupta period stone relief at the Dashavatara Temple in Deogarh depicts Lakshmana wielding a sword and grasping Surpanakha by her hair to sever her facial features.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Another panel depicts Lakshmana cutting off the nose of Surpanakha, the sister of Ravana, for her audacity to propose amours.
facts.text: Archaeological excavations at the 5th-century CE Gupta site of Nachna Kuthara documented narrative stone panels illustrating Rama's forest exile and Lakshmana punishing Surpanakha.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Stratigraphical sequences excavated at Nasik established settled material culture dating back through the Chalcolithic and Early Historic strata.
facts.source_name: Deccan College / ASI, Report on the Excavations at Nasik and Jorwe
facts.text: Excavations conducted in 1950 and 1951 at Nasik, traditionally identified with Panchavati, confirmed human occupation stretching from the Chalcolithic Jorwe phase to Early Historic times.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: A number of authors and commentators have puzzled over the ethically problematic way that Rama and Laksmana treat Surpanakha, an event which ultimately leads to Sita's abduction.
facts.source_name: University of California Press, Many Ramayanas
facts.text: Literary theorists and folklorists debate whether Surpanakha acted as a manipulative instigator seeking revenge against Ravana for her husband's death or was simply a monster punished for an unprovoked physical assault on Sita.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: According to local legend, the place came to be known as Nasik after Lakshmana cut off Surpanakha's nose.
facts.source_name: District Administration of Nashik, Cultural Heritage Records
facts.text: Local oral folklore claims that the city of Nashik acquired its name from the Sanskrit term 'Nasika' because Surpanakha's severed nose was believed to have fallen on that ground.
